title: Seeing God (ST I-II.3.8)
hook: final happiness is seeing God's essence

segments.voice: Yesterday, not money: Thomas tested money, fame, power and pleasure, and found each a real good that can't be the whole of happiness. Your line was none of these. What did you catch yourself chasing? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

A small child in the back seat asks why the sky is blue. You give an answer about sunlight. "Why?" You try something about air. "Why?" A few whys later, every adult in the car is out of answers, and the child is still going. It can be exhausting. Thomas Aquinas treats it as a clue. On his account, that little engine of why doesn't switch off in adults. It just gets quieter, and sometimes gets buried under errands. Yesterday Thomas cleared the table: not money, not fame, not power, not pleasure. Today he says what the will's long hunger is actually for. Seeing God.
screen: `WHY? WHY? WHY?` → `THE ENGINE NEVER SWITCHES OFF.` → `WHAT THE HUNGER IS FOR.`

segments.voice: Thomas's argument starts with wonder. When we see an effect and know it has a cause, we want to know what that cause is. That wanting is wonder, and it doesn't rest until it gets an answer. Follow it all the way up, through every cause, and you arrive at God. Now here's his careful step. Knowing that God exists isn't enough. The arguments we walked through last week can show that there is a first cause. They can't show what God is. And a mind that knows only that, Thomas says, is still asking. The why is still running. So final happiness, for Thomas, can only be one thing: the mind seeing God's very essence, what God is. Not an idea about God. God, seen. The tradition calls it the beatific vision, the seeing that makes blessed. Scripture speaks of it in more than one place. Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." Paul: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." And the First Letter of John: "we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is." Thomas is honest that this isn't something this life delivers. Here, he says, happiness is real but partial. The full thing is a gift, not an achievement. So if an ordinary week leaves a restlessness behind, on Thomas's account it isn't a defect. It's the shape of a person made for something no errand can supply. The child in the back seat is onto something.
screen: `WONDER WANTS THE CAUSE.` · `KNOWING THAT GOD IS: NOT ENOUGH.` · `SEEING WHAT GOD IS.` · `PARTIAL HERE, FULL AS A GIFT.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL SEE GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: long for it, for a minute. Settle, and breathe. Let one question you carry come up. Not a practical one. A big why. Why is there anything? Why do I love the people I love? Why does beauty hurt a little? Don't answer it. Let it stay open, the way a child's why stays open. Notice whether it pulls at you, the wanting to know. Thomas would say that pull is pointing somewhere. You don't have to follow it anywhere today. Just let yourself want, without rushing to fill the want. If you pray, you can say the line from Matthew: they shall see God. The bell holds the time.
Seeing God. For Thomas, final happiness is the mind seeing God's essence, face to face, the vision the tradition calls beatific. Today's word.
Your line: made to see him. Today, when a small restlessness comes, before you fill it with your phone, let it stay for one breath, and wonder what it's for. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics hope for the beatific vision, seeing God face to face, as the final happiness of the saints, and the Church's prayers for the dead and its feast of All Saints speak of this hope.

fork.setup: you're Thomas. you've ruled out money, fame, power and pleasure. a student asks: then what is happiness? what do you answer?
options: the mind seeing what God is, face to face.
feeling peaceful most of the time.
fork.reveal: Thomas says final happiness is the vision of God's essence. knowing only that God exists leaves wonder still asking.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: the vision of the divine essence.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: the argument from wonder, the desire to know the cause of a known effect, and that knowing only that God is leaves desire unrested (I-II.3.8); perfect happiness not possible in this life, imperfect happiness possible (I-II.5.3); perfect happiness as a gift beyond nature (I-II.5.5).
'The arguments we walked through last week' refers to the five ways (days 1156–1158), which fell in the previous week.
'Beatific vision' is the tradition's term, not Thomas's wording in this article; it's attributed to 'the tradition'.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Matthew 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2.

Editor: hook now opens on the scene rather than a quoted question (days 1164 and 1169 also open on quotations); framed the 'engine of why' as Thomas's account; the practice no longer assumes the listener's childhood or tells them what they feel; added I-II.5.5 to sources for 'a gift, not an achievement'.
